title: Prolog
subtitle: Programming in logic: describe what is true, ask questions, and let unification and backtracking find the answers, from a first query to constraint solving.
description: Prolog (PROgrammation en LOGique) was created in 1972 by Alain Colmerauer and Philippe Roussel in Marseille, building on Robert Kowalski's insight that logical statements can be read as procedures. A Prolog program is a set of facts and rules; running it means asking a question, and the system searches for every way of making the question true. Two mechanisms do the work: unification, which matches patterns containing variables, and backtracking, which tries alternatives in order. Prolog shaped artificial intelligence, natural-language processing and expert systems, inspired Datalog and today's rule and query engines, and is still used for parsing, scheduling, verification, configuration and teaching how computation and logic meet.

This course is for anyone who already knows what a variable, a loop and a function are: the Start level of [Lumenary CS](/en/cs/) or equivalent experience in any language. Prolog will ask you to unlearn some habits (there are no loops and no assignment), so no logic background is assumed beyond 'and', 'or' and 'not'. It covers facts, rules and queries, unification, backtracking, recursion over lists, arithmetic, the cut and negation, grammars for parsing, constraint solving, the dynamic database, where Prolog is used today, and a complete puzzle-solving project.

To run the code, install SWI-Prolog, the most widely used free Prolog system, from [swi-prolog.org](https://www.swi-prolog.org/download/stable) (Linux distributions package it as `swi-prolog`; Homebrew as `swi-prolog`). Save a program as `main.pl` and run it with `swipl main.pl`, or start the interactive toplevel with `swipl`. You can also try Prolog without installing anything in [SWISH](https://swish.swi-prolog.org/), SWI-Prolog's official online notebook. Every complete program in these lessons starts with `:- initialization(main, main).`, was run with SWI-Prolog 10.1 by Lumenary's test suite, and shows the output it printed. The lessons were drafted with AI assistance and are awaiting review by a human computer scientist.

levels.title: Facts, unification and search
levels.summary: What logic programming is and where it came from, facts, rules and queries, the unification that matches terms, and the backtracking search that finds every answer.

levels.title: Lists, arithmetic, control and grammars
levels.summary: Recursion over lists with accumulators, arithmetic that is not reversible, the cut and negation as failure, and definite clause grammars for parsing text.

levels.title: Constraints, state and real programs
levels.summary: Solve puzzles with constraint logic programming, manage a dynamic database and tabling, and build a tested, modular puzzle solver while seeing where Prolog and Datalog are used today.
